p01.why: main must not have C language linkage, so most compilers reject; the Evidence says GCC 14 and Clang 18 accept it and the program then runs.

p02.why: The C function is declared in one file and defined in the other under the same C name, so the call links and returns 9.

p03.why: LSP-6 says a pointer to a C function does not convert to a pointer to a C++ function where the type records linkage (EDG), so EDG should reject; Clang and GCC do not record it and compile. The Evidence does not list this case, so this is a guess.

p04.why: Where the type records the linkage, the two take functions are overloads; where it does not, the second line redeclares the same function, which is also valid.

p05.why: A C++ declaration of g is followed by a C declaration of the same function.

p06.why: The two C names item are one entity but one is a variable and one is a function, so they do not agree in kind.

p07.why: A static function in an extern "C" block is allowed and has internal linkage; the call returns 5.

p08.why: A linkage specification can sit in a namespace and the function is found as lib::answer.

p09.why: A C function and a C++ function can overload, so f(1) picks the C one (1) and f(1.0) the C++ one (2).

p10.why: A declaration in braces is a definition as it would be without them, so defined_here is a zero-initialized global and main returns 0.

p11.why: With an initializer the braceless form defines the variable.

p12.why: A C name must not be spelled main, so most compilers reject; the Evidence says GCC 14 and Clang 18 accept a variable named main with C linkage.

p13.why: The matrix compilers support only "C" and "C++" and reject an unknown language.

p14.why: The two C names conflict are one entity but have different types.

p15.why: A later declaration without a linkage specification keeps C linkage, so all three lines name one function; there is no main, so it only compiles.

p16.why: A C name must not share the spelling of a global C++ variable, so most compilers reject; the Evidence says GCC accepts.

p17.why: The braceless form with a body defines the C function; mul(2,3) is 6.

p18.why: The braces make no scope, so visible_after is visible in main and holds 4.

p19.why: A linkage specification must not occur in a block.

p20.why: twice has C linkage, so it matches both the C callback alias and the C parameter type on every compiler; the results are 4 and 10.

p21.why: The braceless form only declares the variable, and nothing defines it.

p22.why: All three declarations of shared are one C entity, defined at global scope; 7 + 7 is 14.

p23.why: Both the function and the variable are defined in the block and visible after it; add(3,1) is 4.

p24.why: The innermost specification is C++, so the two over functions have C++ linkage and overload.

p25.why: The parameter type has C linkage; EDG rejects passing the C++ function plain, while Clang and GCC accept and the program runs.

p26.why: A linkage specification must not occur in a class.

p27.why: The form without braces must not declare a static entity.

p28.why: Two C functions with one name are not overloads.

p29.why: extern "C++" is the default linkage in both forms; these are plain declarations and there is no main.

p30.why: The alias in the extern "C" block is a C function type; EDG rejects the C++ function twice as the argument, while Clang and GCC accept and the program runs.

p31.why: A template must not have C language linkage.

p32.why: Member functions keep C++ linkage inside an extern "C" block, so they can overload; 1 + 2 is 3.
